articles.body:
At the end of every engagement, spend ten minutes recording how it went. Beeline sends a short form when the SOW closes. This is not about managing the contractor's performance — they are not ours to manage — it is about whether we would use them again and whether we scoped the work well.

## What the form asks

* Were the deliverables met, as described in the SOW?
* Was it delivered on time? If not, why — their delay, our delay, or a scope change?
* Was it delivered on budget, and were there revisions? What caused them?
* Quality of the work and of the communication
* Would you engage them again?

**Be honest about our side too.** A late engagement is often our fault — data that was not ready, a reviewer who did not review, a decision that took three weeks. Recording that is more useful than marking the contractor down, because it is the part we can fix.

**Mid-engagement.** On anything running more than a couple of months, have a short check-in at the halfway point: are we on track for the milestones, has the scope moved, is anything blocked on us? Catching a slip halfway is a revision; catching it at the end is a dispute.

**Where quality is a problem.** Raise it with the contractor directly and promptly, pointing at the SOW and the acceptance criteria — this is a commercial conversation, not a performance conversation, and specifics are what make it work. If it does not improve, tell HR before approving any further invoice.

**Where it is a conduct problem** rather than a quality problem — behaviour towards our staff, a confidentiality concern — it goes to HR immediately, the same as it would for anyone. See *Harassment, Discrimination and Safety*.

**What we do with it.** HR keeps the reviews and uses them when someone asks whether we have worked with a supplier before, and when deciding who to approach for similar work. At our size this record is the whole of our institutional memory about suppliers, so a two-line answer that says nothing helps nobody.

Separate contractor delay from Helvia-caused blockers or scope changes. Raise quality issues promptly with the contractor using the SOW and acceptance criteria; this is a commercial delivery discussion, not an employee performance process. If quality does not improve, tell HR before approving another invoice. Conduct, confidentiality, harassment, or safety concerns go to HR immediately. HR retains the final Beeline review as the organization’s supplier history, so record specific evidence rather than a vague score.

## Training they should have:

Anything needed to do the work safely and properly.

*   **Safety training for their site or task** — required before the work starts, no exceptions
*   **Security and data handling** — required for anyone with access to our systems
*   **Tool and process training specific to how we work** — our deployment process, our ticketing conventions, our house style
*   **Compliance training where the role requires it**

Book this the way you would for anyone in the team. For contingent workers, tell the agency if the training takes significant time, because it is billable — the worker is being paid for those hours.

## Training we do not provide:

General professional development, certifications, conference attendance, management or leadership training, and anything aimed at the person's career rather than the work in front of them. That belongs
to their employer, and offering it blurs the line — paying for someone's certification looks a lot like investing in an employee.

[[PAGE_END]]

## Team building

If the whole team is doing it and it is about how the team works together, external workers are included. If attendance is required, contingent workers are paid for the time.

## Where an external worker asks for development support

Be straightforward: explain that it comes from their own employer, and point them there. For a contingent worker the agency often does provide training, so this is a real answer rather than a brush-off.

## Records

Safety and compliance training completion is recorded on the BambooHR record. HR checks it periodically, and an assignment where required training has not been done will be paused until it is.

## Instructors

Where an external worker has the expertise to run a session for our team, that is fine and often valuable — but it should be within the scope of the assignment or SOW, not a favour. For contractors, if it is not in the SOW, revise the SOW.

articles.body:
Everyone working at Helvia is entitled to a workplace free of harassment, discrimination and violence — external workers included, and whether the person raising the concern is one of ours or one of theirs.

### If something is raised with you, or you see it:

1. **Report it the same day** to HR, at hr@helvia.ai or in person. If the concern involves HR, go to the CEO.
2. **Do not investigate it yourself.** Do not interview people, gather statements, or test the story. Well-meant digging contaminates a proper investigation and can make things worse for the person who spoke up.
3. **Do not promise confidentiality you cannot keep.** Tell them it will be handled discreetly and shared only with those who need to know.
4. **Write down what you were told**, in their words, with the date, and give it to HR.

HR will decide what kind of investigation is needed, involve the agency where a contingent worker is on either side, involve the contractor's company where a contractor is, and take advice where the matter is serious.

**Where there is an immediate safety risk, act first:** separate the people involved, and call emergency services if anyone is in danger. Then call HR.

**Retaliation is prohibited.** Nobody who raises a concern in good faith, or takes part in an investigation, should see any consequence for it — not a changed shift, not a quieter assignment, not an assignment that quietly ends. This applies to external workers exactly as it does to employees, and ending someone's assignment shortly after they raised something is precisely the pattern that creates liability. Talk to HR before making any change to the assignment of someone who has raised a concern.

**Our size does not exempt us.** The federal rules on discrimination and harassment apply to employers with 15 or more employees, and state law in several of the states we operate in sets a lower bar still. Assume we are covered.

---

Retaliation is prohibited for anyone raising or supporting a concern. Do not change shifts, assignments, duties, or end an engagement after a report without HR review. External workers receive the same protection, and Helvia’s size does not remove the applicable federal or state obligations.

Everyone working for us must have the right to work in the country where they are doing the work. Who checks depends on the track.

* **Track 1 — contingent workers.** The agency is the employer and carries the obligation. They verify right to work and complete the I-9 before the assignment starts. We do not collect or keep immigration documents for agency workers — that is their employer's job, and holding the paperwork ourselves blurs exactly the line we are trying to keep clear. HR confirms with the agency that checks are done; that confirmation is what we record.
* **Track 2 — contractors.** A contractor company is responsible for its own people. For an independent contractor working as an individual, HR confirms their right to work as part of onboarding.

**Visa sponsorship.** We do not sponsor visas for external workers on either track. If an agency puts forward someone who needs sponsorship now or later, the agency sponsors and carries the cost, or the candidate is not eligible for the assignment. Say so in the request so the agency does not waste time.

**If the role genuinely needs someone we would sponsor**, that is a conversation about hiring an employee, not about the external workforce. Talk to HR.

**Support letters.** Occasionally an agency asks us to confirm in writing that someone is on assignment with us. HR writes those letters — they confirm the assignment and nothing more. Do not write one yourself; a letter that overstates the relationship is evidence of the wrong thing.

---

**A confidentiality agreement is in place.** For contingent workers this sits in our agreement with the agency and covers everyone they place. For contractors it is in the contract. HR confirms it before access is granted — no agreement, no access, regardless of how urgent the work is.

**We own what they produce.** Anything created for us in the course of the work belongs to Helvia. This is explicit in both the agency agreement and the contractor contract, and it needs to be, because the default position in law is often the opposite for contractors: absent a written assignment, a freelancer may retain

[[PAGE_END]]

copyright in what they build. For anything involving code, design, written content or product IP, check with HR that the contract carries a proper assignment clause before work starts.

### In practice

* Give access to what the job needs, and nothing more. Ask IT for the narrowest role that works.
* Do not share customer data, financial results or roadmap material outside the scope of the assignment.
* Anything an external worker builds goes into our repositories and our accounts, not their personal ones.
* Where a contractor is using their own tooling, agree up front where the work lives and how it is handed over. "It is on my laptop" at the end of an engagement is a bad place to start a conversation.
* Access is removed the day the assignment ends. See the offboarding sections of both process guides.

**Where an external worker will see personal data** about our customers or staff, tell HR at the request stage. There may be a data processing agreement to put in place first.

---

articles.body:
The bill rate is what we pay the agency per hour for a contingent worker. It is not what the worker takes home — the agency's employment costs, taxes, benefits and margin all come out of it. A bill rate roughly 1.4 to 1.6 times the equivalent hourly wage is normal, and it is not a markup to be negotiated away; it is the cost of someone else carrying the employment relationship.

**Who sets it.** HR agrees rates with our agencies and reviews them annually against the market. Rates are set per role, not per person, so two people doing the same job come in at the same rate.

**Managers do not negotiate rates.** Not with the agency, not with the worker. If a rate looks wrong for the market, or an agency pushes back on a role, tell HR — they will look at it. Agreeing something directly undercuts every other assignment we have and damages a relationship we depend on.

**Rate changes mid-assignment are unusual.** They happen where the role has genuinely changed, or at the annual review for a long-running assignment. They go through HR and need the same approval as an extension.

**Contractor pricing works differently:** a fixed fee or milestone payments agreed in the SOW, or capped time and materials where the work genuinely cannot be scoped. See Contract and Statement of Work.

**What the worker earns is between them and their employer.** If a contingent worker tells you they are unhappy with their pay, or asks what we are paying the agency:
* do not tell them the bill rate
* do not offer an opinion on whether their pay is fair
* point them to their agency contact
* tell HR if it sounds like something is genuinely wrong

That last point matters. Occasionally a worker raises something that is a real problem — being paid below the agreed rate, or not being paid at all. Do not investigate it, but do pass it to HR the same day.

**Budgeting.** Beeline shows committed and actual spend per assignment. A rough planning figure: a contingent worker at $60/hour bill rate, full time, costs about $10,400 a month. Check Assignment Spend before extending anyone.

---

articles.body:
These rules apply to contingent workers, who are paid hourly. Contractors are paid against a SOW and none of this applies to them.

**Overtime.** Anything over 40 hours in a week is paid at 1.5 times the regular rate. This is federal law under the FLSA and it applies to us at any headcount.

Two of our states count overtime by the day as well:

[[PAGE_END]]

| State | Daily overtime | Double time |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **California** | 1.5× beyond 8 hours in a day, up to 12 | 2× beyond 12 hours in a day, and beyond 8 hours on the seventh consecutive day worked in a week |
| **Colorado** | 1.5× beyond 12 hours in a day | — |
| **Illinois** | Weekly only | — |
| **Texas** | Weekly only | — |

So a worker in California doing four 10-hour days is owed overtime for 8 hours, even though the week totals 40. A worker in Texas doing the same is not. Beeline applies the right rule from the worker's recorded state, which is why keeping their location accurate matters.

**Overtime must be agreed in advance.** Not because it is optional to pay — it is not, once worked — but because it is your budget and you should know. If overtime appears on a timesheet you did not approve, reject it and talk to the worker and the agency.

**Double time on holidays.** Where a contingent worker is asked to work on one of our recognised holidays, the assignment can provide for double time. This is agreed in advance with HR and the agency, not decided in the moment.

**Compensatory time is not allowed.** You cannot give a contingent worker time off next week instead of paying this week's overtime. It is unlawful for non-exempt workers in the private sector, and it is one of the easiest things for a regulator to find. Every hour worked goes on the timesheet, under the right code, and is paid in the week it was worked.

**Exempt workers.** A small number of contingent assignments are for exempt roles, where the agency bills a flat 40-hour week regardless of hours worked. The agency determines exempt status, not us, and HR will tell you before the assignment starts if it applies.

---

articles.body:
Work time is any time a worker spends on something that benefits us or that we require — whether or not anyone asked them to do it, and whether or not it happens at their desk.

This matters because every hour of work time must be paid, at no less than minimum wage, with overtime where it applies. The agency is responsible for paying it, but we are the ones creating the hours, so the way we manage people determines the bill.

### Counts as work time

* the obvious: doing the job
* required training, and required meetings
* travel between work sites during the day
* short breaks of 20 minutes or less — always paid, never deducted
* being on site and required to be available, even if it is quiet

[[PAGE_END]]

* work done outside normal hours because we asked it, including answering messages in the evening

### Does not count

* commuting from home to their normal place of work
* a genuine meal break of 30 minutes or more where they are completely free of duties
* time entirely their own, with no expectation of availability

**The trap.** "Just check your email before you log on" and "stay by the phone in case" are both work time. If you expect availability, you are buying hours. Be explicit with contingent workers about when they are and are not working — vagueness here is how unpaid work happens, and it is the worker who pays for it.

**Short breaks are paid.** A ten-minute break, a coffee, a step outside — paid, and not deducted from anything. This is federal law, not a courtesy.

**Meal breaks can be unpaid,** but only if all of these are true: the break is at least 30 minutes; the worker is completely relieved of duties, which means not eating at their desk while covering the queue; and they are generally free to leave. Eating while nominally on call does not qualify — that is a paid break.

**If a break is interrupted,** it becomes work time and the worker should record it. Tell them that explicitly, because most people will not.

**Anything under 30 minutes** that you are thinking of treating as an unpaid break is not one. Ask HR before you do.

---

We currently have people in **California, Colorado, Illinois and Texas.** State rules apply based on where the worker physically does the work, not where we are based — so a remote worker in California gets California's rules.

| | California | Colorado | Illinois | Texas |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Meal break** | 30 min, unpaid, starting before the end of hour 5. A second 30 min before the end of hour 10 on shifts over 10 hours — waivable if the shift finishes within 12 | 30 min, unpaid, on shifts over 5 hours. Not in the first or last hour where practical | 20 min, unpaid, on shifts of 7½ hours or more, taken before the end of hour 5. Another 20 min for each further 4½ hours | No state requirement |
| **Rest breaks** | Paid 10 min for every 4 hours, or major fraction. Roughly the middle of each block | Paid 10 min for every 4 hours. 1 break on shifts over 2 up to 6 hours, 2 up to 10 hours, 3 up to 14 hours | No state requirement | No state requirement |
| **Weekly rest** | — | — | 24 consecutive hours off in every 7 days | — |

[[PAGE_END]]

| | California | Colorado | Illinois | Texas |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Missed break penalty** | 1 hour's pay per day for a missed meal, and another for a missed rest break | 10 minutes' pay per missed rest break | — | — |

**Texas and the federal baseline.** Texas has no state meal or rest law. Federal rules still apply: short breaks of 20 minutes or less are paid, and a meal break can only be unpaid if it meets the conditions in What Counts as Work Time.

**California is the one to watch.** The penalties are per day and they add up quickly — a worker who misses both a meal and a rest break is owed two extra hours of pay for that day. The common cause is a well-meant "just push through lunch, we're slammed". Do not do it, and make sure whoever covers for you knows not to either.

### Practical rules for managers

* Build breaks into the shift. Do not rely on people taking them.
* Never ask someone to skip or shorten a break. Never imply it.
* If a break gets interrupted, tell them to record it as work time.
* Cover matters: if there is nobody to hand over to, the break will not happen.

**Any other state.** If we place someone anywhere outside these four, the rules will be different. Tell HR before the assignment starts — do not assume the nearest state's rules apply, and do not assume the federal baseline is enough.

Ordinary commuting and a duty-free meal of at least 30 minutes are not work time; an interrupted meal becomes paid time. Overtime must be approved in advance but must still be paid once worked, and compensatory time is prohibited. Federal weekly overtime applies beyond 40 hours; California and Colorado also have daily rules, and Beeline uses the recorded work state. California requires meal and paid rest breaks with one-hour pay penalties for missed meals and another hour for missed rest; Colorado, Illinois, and Texas differ. Build breaks into shifts, record interruptions, and consult HR before placing someone in an unlisted state.

articles.body:
Every external worker gets a BambooHR record, created by HR once the assignment or SOW is confirmed in Beeline. It is the single answer to "who is this person and are they meant to be here".

### What is on the record

* name, work email and start date
* worker type: Contingent or Contractor
* the agency or contractor company
* the hiring manager
* the assignment or SOW end date
* location and, for remote workers, which state
* confirmation that right-to-work checks and any background check are complete

**What is deliberately not on it:** salary or bill rate, which sits in Beeline; anything about their employment with the agency; medical or accommodation detail, which HR holds separately and confidentially; and personal documents, which stay with their employer.

**Why the end date matters.** IT works from BambooHR. The end date is what drives account expiry, so an assignment extended in Beeline but not reflected in BambooHR means an account that closes mid-assignment — and an assignment ended in Beeline but not closed properly means an account that never closes at all. HR keeps the two in step, which is why closing things properly in Beeline matters.

**What managers can see.** Your own team, including external workers: who they are, who they work for, when their assignment ends, and how to contact them. You cannot see other teams' external workers, and nobody outside HR sees pay data.

**External workers' own access.** Contingent workers get a limited BambooHR account so they appear in the directory and can find people. They have no time-off, benefits or payroll functions — those belong to their employer. Contractors normally get no BambooHR account at all.

**The directory.** External workers appear with their worker type and their agency or company shown. This is deliberate: anyone looking at the directory should be able to tell immediately who is employed by us and who is not.

**Corrections** go to `hr@helvia.ai`. Do not work around a wrong record — a wrong manager or end date has consequences downstream.

articles.body:
**Notifications.** Beeline emails you when something needs your attention: a timesheet or invoice to approve, candidates ready to review, a request approved or rejected, an assignment ending in 30 days, or a check-in form due.

[[PAGE_END]]

Leave them on. You can turn them off under **Settings → Notifications**, but then you have to remember to look, and the thing that gets missed is always a timesheet approval — which delays someone's pay. If the volume is the problem, a mail rule filing them into a folder works better than switching them off.

**The one to keep.** If you turn everything else off, keep the timesheet approval notification. It is the only one with a hard deadline attached and a person on the other end of it.

**Delegates.** A delegate acts for you in Beeline while you are away: approving timesheets, expenses and invoices. Set one under **Settings → Delegates**, choose the person, and set a date range — you can do this weeks ahead, and it switches itself on and off.

Your delegate should be someone who knows the work well enough to spot a wrong timesheet. Delegating to someone who will approve everything without looking removes the only control in the chain.

**What a delegate cannot do:** raise new requests on your behalf, approve above your threshold, or change an assignment. Those wait for you, or go to your manager.

### Before any leave longer than a couple of days

* Set a delegate in Beeline with the right dates
* Tell them what is likely to land and anything unusual to watch for
* Deal with anything already in your queue before you go
* Check Upcoming End Dates for anything expiring while you are away, and extend it now

**If you leave Helvia or change role**, your assignments need reassigning to a new manager — HR handles this, but tell them, because assignments pointing at someone who has gone are approvals nobody is doing and end dates nobody is watching.

articles.body:
# Travel and Expenses

**PEOPLE OPERATIONS · POLICY**

When external workers travel, how they get paid back, and what can and cannot be claimed.

**Audience** Hiring managers, HR and Finance

**Classification** Internal use only

[[PAGE_END]]

## Rules for External Workers

External workers travel only where the work genuinely requires it, and it should be agreed before anything is booked.

**The rule that catches people out: external workers do not get a Helvia credit card and do not book through our accounts.** They pay for travel themselves, claim it back from their own employer, and their employer bills us. This applies to both tracks, and it applies to flights, hotels, car hire and rail alike.

The reason is not administrative. Putting an external worker on our corporate card and our travel account makes them look like our employee — it is one of the clearest co-employment signals there is.

**Track 1 — contingent workers.** Where travel is needed, agree it with the worker in advance and tell HR so the agency knows to expect the claim. The worker claims from the agency; the agency bills us at cost. Travel time during the working day is work time and is paid.

**Track 2 — contractors.** Travel is reimbursable only if the SOW says so. Agree the rules when you write the SOW: normally travel and accommodation at cost with receipts, and nothing else. A contractor who travels without it being in the SOW has no route to be paid for it.

**Booking sensibly.** We expect the same judgement we would apply to ourselves: book ahead rather than at the last minute, economy on flights, a reasonable hotel near the work. Nobody needs to find the absolute cheapest option, but nobody should be booking a flexible fare a day out without a reason.

**International travel** for a contingent worker is possible but tightly bounded: it must be initiated by us, agreed by the worker and the agency, and last no more than 10 business days. Anything longer raises tax and work-authorisation questions in the destination country. Talk to HR well in advance — this needs lead time.

**Travelling is not the same as working abroad.** A short business trip is fine. Doing the day job from another country is not. See Working From Outside the United States.

**Safety.** Anyone travelling on our business should have a way to reach us and we should know roughly where they are. For anything beyond routine domestic travel, tell HR the destination and dates.

## What Can and Cannot Be Claimed

This is what we will reimburse when an external worker travels on our business — via their employer for contingent workers, or per the SOW for contractors.

| | Reimbursable | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Travel** | | |
| Flights, economy | Yes | Book ahead where possible |
| Rail, standard class | Yes | |
| Checked baggage | Yes | One bag |

[[PAGE_END]]

| | Reimbursable | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Seat upgrades, lounge access, airline memberships | No | |
| Car hire | Yes, where it is the sensible option | Mid-size or smaller |
| Fuel for a hire car | Yes | Return it full |
| Taxis, rideshare, public transport | Yes | |
| Mileage in their own car | Yes, at the standard IRS rate | Only where agreed in advance |
| Parking and tolls | Yes | |
| Commuting to their normal workplace | No | Including mileage and parking |
| **Accommodation** | | |
| Hotel room and tax | Yes | Reasonable standard, near the work |
| Hotel on the night of an overnight flight | Yes | |
| Room service movies, minibar, spa, gym | No | |
| Late cancellation or no-show | Yes, if unavoidable | Cancel in time where you can |
| **Meals** | | |
| Own meals while travelling overnight | Yes | Reasonable, with receipts |
| A meal with a customer or partner | Yes | Note who attended and why |
| Alcohol | Only with a meal, in moderation | |
| Meals on a normal working day at their usual location | No | |
| **Other** | | |
| Laundry on trips over 7 days | Yes | |
| Tips, reasonable | Yes | |
| Wi-Fi and phone charges needed for work | Yes | |
| Visa and entry fees for required travel | Yes | |
| Travel insurance, medical costs, vaccinations | No | Their employer's responsibility |
| Family or partner travel | No | |

[[PAGE_END]]

| | Reimbursable | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fines, penalties and parking tickets | No | |
| Personal items, toiletries, entertainment | No | |

**Receipts.** Every line needs one. Claims arrive through the agency or on a contractor invoice, and Finance will query anything without support.

**Timing.** Claims should reach us within 30 days of the trip. Late claims still get paid but they make budget tracking painful.

**If something is not on this list,** ask before spending rather than after. finance@helvia.ai for whether it is claimable, hr@helvia.ai for whether it is appropriate.

topics.backgroundKnowledge: External-worker travel must be genuinely required and agreed before booking. Workers do not receive Helvia cards or use Helvia travel accounts; they pay, claim from their employer, and the employer bills Helvia. For Track 1, notify HR and the agency; daytime travel is paid work time. Contractor travel is reimbursable only when the SOW permits it. Use sensible advance booking, economy flights, standard rail, reasonable hotels, and receipts for every line. Normal commuting, upgrades, lounges, personal entertainment, family travel, medical costs, insurance, and fines are not reimbursable; some items such as car hire, mileage, alcohol with a meal, cancellations, and longer-trip laundry are conditional. Claims should arrive within 30 days. A Helvia-initiated international trip for a contingent worker requires agency agreement and must not exceed 10 business days; ordinary working abroad is prohibited.
